preview_text: ใน TCM มะเร็งลำไส้ใหญ่และทวารหนักไม่ใช่โรคเดียว แต่มีรูปแบบที่แตกต่างกันหลายรูปแบบ และการรักษาที่กำจัด Damp-Heat นั้นแตกต่างอย่างมากจากการรักษาที่สร้าง Qi และเลือดขึ้นใหม่หลังจากนั้น...
categories: ["เนื้องอกและมะเร็ง", "ปัญหาลำไส้และลำไส้"]
conventional_description: Colorectal cancer is a malignancy that begins in the colon or rectum, often developing from precancerous polyps over many years. Common symptoms include a persistent change in bowel habits, blood in the stool, abdominal discomfort, unexplained weight loss, and fatigue. Diagnosis is typically made through colonoscopy with biopsy, and staging is determined by imaging scans to guide treatment decisions.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment depends on the stage and may include surgery to remove the tumor, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. These approaches aim to eliminate cancer cells, shrink tumors, and prevent recurrence, but they can also come with significant side effects like nausea, fatigue, neuropathy, and lowered blood counts.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, colorectal cancer is understood as a complex interplay between deficiency and excess. The root is almost always a weakness of the Spleen and Stomach, the organs responsible for transforming food into Qi and Blood. When the Spleen is weak, it fails to manage fluids, leading to the accumulation of Dampness. Over time, this Dampness can combine with Heat - often from a diet rich in greasy, spicy, or sweet foods - and settle in the Large Intestine, creating a toxic environment where masses can form.
But the Spleen is only part of the story. The Kidneys, which store the body's fundamental vitality, and the Liver, which ensures the smooth flow of Qi, are also deeply involved.
Long-standing emotional stress, overwork, or constitutional weakness can drain the Kidneys and cause the Liver to stagnate. When Qi stagnates, Blood cannot flow properly, and it congeals into stasis - a key factor in tumor formation. So a cancerous mass is seen not as a foreign invader, but as a local manifestation of a systemic imbalance: a tangle of Dampness, Heat, Blood stasis, and toxic accumulation rooted in a weakened constitution.
This is why a single Western diagnosis can present so differently in different people. One person may have urgent, bloody stools with a burning sensation and a thick yellow tongue coating (Damp-Heat), while another is pale, exhausted, and has loose stools with a poor appetite (Spleen Qi Deficiency).
A third may feel a fixed, stabbing pain and have a dark purple tongue (Blood Stagnation). Each pattern requires a fundamentally different herbal formula and acupuncture strategy, even though they all fall under the same diagnosis of colorectal cancer.
classical_quote: 「肠覃者，寒气客于肠外，与卫气相搏... 息肉乃生。」
classical_translation: "Intestinal mass (chang tan) arises when cold Qi lodges outside the intestine and struggles with the defensive Qi... polyps then grow. This is one of the earliest descriptions of a progressive abdominal mass resembling colorectal cancer."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing (Su Wen)  ,  Chapter 40: Discussion on Abdominal Disorders 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what brought you to seek help - the quality of the stool, the nature of the pain, and the overall energy level. These clues point toward which pattern is driving the illness. Because colorectal cancer often involves a mix of root deficiency and branch excess, the practitioner also looks at your tongue and feels your pulse to confirm which aspect is most active at this moment.
If the main picture is acute: stools with blood and mucus, a burning sensation in the anus, urgent need to go, and a red tongue with a thick yellow greasy coating, the dominant pattern is Damp-Heat in the Large Intestine. A slippery, rapid pulse supports this. In contrast, chronic fatigue, poor appetite, loose or unformed stools, and a pale tongue with tooth marks point to Spleen Qi Deficiency - the root weakness that allowed the damp-heat to accumulate in the first place.
When the pain is fixed in one spot, feels stabbing or boring, and you can sometimes feel a mass, the pattern is Blood Stagnation. The tongue is dark purple or has purplish spots, and the pulse is choppy or wiry. As the disease consumes the body’s resources, you may see profound pallor, weight loss, and extreme fatigue - this shifts the diagnosis toward Qi and Blood Deficiency, with a pale, thin tongue and a weak, thready pulse.
In later stages or after prolonged chemotherapy, you might notice a dry mouth, night sweats, a feeling of heat in the palms and soles, and a red tongue with little or no coating. This indicates Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency, where the body’s cooling and nourishing fluids have been deeply damaged. A thin, rapid pulse confirms this yin-deficient picture.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bloody stools with mucus", "Urgent, incomplete bowel movements (tenesmus)", "Burning sensation at the anus", "Foul-smelling, yellow-brown diarrhea", "Abdominal cramping and pain", "Feeling of heaviness in the body", "Thirst with a desire to drink", "Poor appetite and nausea"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried foods, Spicy or rich food, Alcohol and coffee, Emotional frustration or anger, Damp or humid weather
patterns.better_with: Light, cooling foods, Adequate hydration, Gentle movement or exercise, Rest during flare-ups, Cool, dry weather
patterns.why_this_happens: When Spleen Qi is weak, it fails to transform and transport fluids, leading to an accumulation of Dampness. Over time, this Dampness combines with Heat-often from a diet rich in greasy, spicy, or sweet foods, or from emotional stress-and settles in the Large Intestine. This toxic Damp-Heat mixture irritates the bowel lining, causing the bloody stools, mucus, and urgent, painful bowel movements that are often the first alarming signs of colorectal cancer. The persistent inflammation and stagnation create a fertile environment where masses can form.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, thickest in the center and root. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and rich foods directly introduce Dampness and Heat into the body, overwhelming the already weak Spleen and fueling the toxic accumulation in the bowel. Alcohol and coffee add pure Heat, while stress causes Liver Qi to stagnate and turn into Heat, which then invades the Spleen and worsens Dampness. Cooling, water-rich foods and hydration help clear Heat and flush out Dampness through urine, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids circulating so they don't stagnate. A hot, humid environment mirrors the internal pattern and makes the body feel even heavier and more sluggish.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and overly sweet foods, as well as alcohol and coffee-these all generate Dampness and Heat. Focus on light, easily digestible meals with cooling, water-rich vegetables like cucumber, celery, and bok choy. Cooked grains like barley and millet help drain Dampness. Gentle, regular movement such as walking or tai chi supports Spleen Qi and prevents stagnation, but rest during acute flare-ups.

patterns.symptoms: ["Poor appetite and early satiety", "Bloating and discomfort after eating", "Chronic loose, unformed stools", "Deep fatigue and heaviness in limbs", "Pale complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and fatigue, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Greasy, heavy, or sugary foods, Skipping meals, Damp or humid weather, Emotional stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Warm, easily digested meals, Small frequent meals, Rest and adequate sleep, Gentle movement or exercise, Warm compress on abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is the engine of digestion and Qi production. When Spleen Qi is weak, food is not properly transformed, leading to chronic loose stools, bloating, and deep fatigue. Over years, this deficiency allows Dampness and turbidity to accumulate in the Large Intestine, creating a foundation for tumor growth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: soft and weak, especially at the right guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and regular, moderate nourishment. Overwork and stress drain Qi, while raw, cold, and heavy foods demand extra digestive fire that a deficient Spleen cannot provide. Warm, easily digested meals and rest allow the Spleen to rebuild its Qi, which is essential for transforming food into energy and preventing the accumulation of Dampness that fuels tumor growth.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize warm, cooked foods such as rice congee, soups, and stewed vegetables that are easy on digestion. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy dishes that further weaken the Spleen. Eat small, frequent meals rather than large heavy ones. Rest is essential; avoid overwork and get sufficient sleep. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi can help Qi flow without depleting energy.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi flow in the abdomen is blocked for a long time-often due to Spleen deficiency and lingering Dampness-blood cannot move freely and begins to congeal in the large intestine. This stagnant blood gradually hardens into a palpable tumor mass and produces a fixed, stabbing pain that does not shift location. The stasis also damages local vessels, leading to dark blood in the stool, and the classic dark-purple tongue reflects the deep-seated blood blockage.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple or dusky body, possible stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩, Sè), rough like a knife scraping bamboo, often with a wiry (弦, Xián) quality.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stagnation arises when Qi is obstructed and fails to move blood. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, directly worsening blood stasis. Cold and raw foods constrict vessels and slow circulation, while prolonged sitting and overwork stagnate Qi in the lower abdomen. Gentle movement, warmth, and stress reduction encourage smooth Qi flow and blood circulation, helping to dissolve stasis and ease pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize warm, lightly cooked meals and avoid cold, raw foods that constrict blood vessels. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi keeps Qi and blood circulating, while prolonged sitting should be avoided. A warm compress over the lower abdomen can ease pain. Manage emotional stress to prevent Liver Qi from tightening and worsening stasis.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and fatigue, Raw, cold, or greasy foods, Chemotherapy and major surgery, Emotional stress and worry

patterns.why_this_happens:
Colorectal cancer is a consuming disease. The tumor itself, as well as surgery and chemotherapy, drain the body's Qi and Blood over time. The Spleen, which is responsible for making Qi and Blood from food, becomes too weak to replenish the losses, so the body slides into a state of profound depletion.
Without enough Qi to energize and enough Blood to nourish, every system slows down. This is why people feel bone-deep fatigue, look pale, and often lose weight. The large intestine also loses its tone and function, leading to lingering digestive weakness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or show teeth marks on the edges, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, or empty and forceless.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are the body's fundamental energy and nourishment. Rest and warm, easily digested foods support the Spleen, which is the factory for making more Qi and Blood. Overwork, stress, and taxing treatments like chemotherapy drain these resources faster than they can be replenished, deepening the deficiency. Gentle movement helps Qi flow without depleting it, while raw and cold foods weaken the Spleen's digestive fire, making it even harder to rebuild strength.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, easily digestible foods that gently build Qi and Blood, like congee with a little bone broth, slow-cooked stews, and well-cooked root vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Rest is medicine - prioritize sleep and short, gentle walks rather than pushing through fatigue.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency often appears in the later stages of colorectal cancer, or after prolonged chemotherapy and radiation. These treatments, along with the cancer itself, consume the body's cooling, moistening Yin fluids. When the Kidneys and Liver run dry, deficiency heat flares up, leading to the hallmark dry mouth, night sweats, and a red, peeled tongue.
Without enough Yin to anchor the mind and nourish the tissues, dizziness, insomnia, and lower back soreness develop. The large intestine also loses its lubrication, which can worsen constipation and abdominal discomfort.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red, thin body with cracks; little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: Fine, rapid, and often wiry; weak in the left Chi (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, moistening substance. Spicy foods, alcohol, and emotional heat burn up Yin, while late nights and overwork drain the Kidneys. Rest, hydration, and nourishing foods like pears and congee replenish Yin fluids, calming the deficiency heat that causes night sweats, dry mouth, and restlessness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, easy-to-digest foods like pear, congee, tofu, and black sesame. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods, alcohol, and coffee. Gentle movement like tai chi or walking helps Qi flow without overexertion. Prioritize rest and a cool, quiet sleep environment to preserve Yin.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat colorectal cancer instead of surgery or chemotherapy?
faqs.answer: No. TCM should not be used as a substitute for conventional cancer treatment. Surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation are the primary, evidence-based approaches for treating colorectal cancer. TCM is best used as a complementary therapy to support your body during conventional treatment, reduce side effects, and strengthen your constitution to aid recovery and potentially lower the risk of recurrence.

faqs.question: How can TCM help during chemotherapy?
faqs.answer: TCM is widely used in China to reduce the side effects of chemotherapy. Herbal formulas can help manage nausea, vomiting, fatigue, poor appetite, and low white blood cell counts. Acupuncture is also effective for chemotherapy-induced nausea and pain. By supporting the Spleen and Stomach and nourishing Qi and Blood, TCM helps patients maintain their strength and complete their full course of treatment with a better quality of life.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my cancer medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but it must be done under the guidance of a qualified TCM practitioner who is experienced in oncology. Some herbs can interact with chemotherapy drugs or blood thinners, so it’s crucial to inform both your oncologist and your TCM practitioner about everything you are taking. A knowledgeable practitioner will choose formulas that are safe and supportive, avoiding herbs that might interfere with your treatment.

faqs.question: What diet does TCM recommend for colorectal cancer?
faqs.answer: The general principle is to avoid foods that create Dampness and Heat - greasy, fried, spicy, and overly sweet foods, as well as alcohol. Raw and cold foods should be limited because they weaken the Spleen. Instead, focus on warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, steamed vegetables, and well-cooked grains. Foods that gently strengthen the Spleen, such as rice, oats, sweet potato, and carrots, are especially beneficial.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with cancer pain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can be an effective part of a pain management plan for colorectal cancer, especially when pain is related to surgery, tumor pressure, or nerve involvement. It works by promoting the flow of Qi and Blood, reducing stagnation, and triggering the release of the body’s natural pain-relieving endorphins. It is often used alongside conventional pain medications to reduce the needed dosage and minimize side effects.

faqs.question: How long does TCM treatment for colorectal cancer take?
faqs.answer: This depends on your goals. If you are using TCM to manage chemotherapy side effects, you may feel better within 2 to 4 weeks. For rebuilding strength and vitality after treatment, a course of 3 to 6 months is common. Long-term prevention of recurrence often involves periodic herbal formulas and seasonal acupuncture check-ups over several years. Your practitioner will adjust the plan based on your progress and changing pattern.

research.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine for Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
research.description: This meta-analysis of 20 RCTs found that adding Chinese herbal medicine to conventional chemotherapy improved overall survival and quality of life, and reduced the incidence of chemotherapy-related side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and leukopenia.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2017.

research.title: Acupuncture for Cancer-Related Fatigue in Patients with Colorectal Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
research.description: In this trial, 302 colorectal cancer patients received acupuncture or usual care. Acupuncture significantly reduced fatigue levels and improved physical functioning, with benefits maintained at 18-week follow-up.
research.periodical: Molassiotis A, et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2012;30(36):4470-4476.

research.title: Effect of Jianpi Jiedu Recipe on Survival and Immune Function in Patients with Colorectal Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
research.description: This study showed that a Spleen-strengthening and toxin-resolving herbal formula prolonged disease-free survival and enhanced immune markers such as CD3+ and CD4+ T cells in stage III colorectal cancer patients after surgery and chemotherapy.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2019;25(3):172-179.
